placeFacts.title: The places at a glance
placeFacts.intro: Who do the numbers in the table belong to? Here is a short answer.

about.municipality: The figures of the municipality of {name} ({canton}), without the canton.
about.canton: The figures of the canton of {canton} itself, without its municipalities.
about.cantonRest: All municipalities of the canton of {canton} with fewer than 5,000 inhabitants, together. Not published but calculated: the canton minus the individual municipalities.

placeFacts.note: Values refer to the year of the dataset. If there is no value for that year, the closest year is shown.

explain.title: How to read the numbers
explain.hint: Briefly explained: balance sheet, revenue, expenses and more

rows.title: What do the rows mean?
rows.balance: Balance sheet: what a place owns (assets) and where the money for it came from (liabilities: debt and equity). Both sides are always equal.
rows.income: Income statement: what comes in during a year (revenue, mostly taxes and fees) and what is spent (expenses, for example on staff, schools and social services).
rows.result: Profit/loss is revenue minus expenses. A minus means more was spent than received.
rows.expand: Tap an arrow to open a row into its parts.

scaling.title: Why "per inhabitant"?
scaling.text: Big places almost always have bigger amounts. Pick "Population" below and every amount is divided by the number of inhabitants. That makes places of different sizes comparable. The same works per job, per kilometre of road and more.

compare.title: Compare two columns
compare.text: Tap a column heading as the base, then a second one. You will see by how many percent the second one differs.

source.title: Where do the numbers come from?
source.text: The financial figures come from the Swiss Federal Finance Administration (FFA). Municipalities are included from 5,000 inhabitants. The latest years may still be provisional and change later. Inhabitants, jobs and roads come from the Federal Statistical Office.

limits.title: Things to keep in mind
limits.text: Cantons and municipalities do not book everything the same way, and tasks are shared out differently: sometimes the municipality pays for schools, sometimes the canton. A difference in the table shows that something is different, but not always why.

editor.name: Scenario name

presetHint.both: All main accounts of expenses and revenue (30–38, 40–48) together.

modeHint.ols: Weights may be negative. Closest fit, harder to interpret.
modeHint.nonneg: All weights are ≥ 0: every factor can only enlarge the formula. Recommended.
modeHint.robust: Like non-negative, but a single outlier (e.g. one big city) hardly distorts the result.

editor.autoSelectHint: Picks the smallest factor combination with the best cross-validated error. With few places this protects against overfitting.
editor.intercept: Constant base term in the formula
editor.interceptHint: Off: the formula is proportional to the factors. On: a fixed base the same for every place (costs one degree of freedom).
editor.ridgeHint: Pulls the weights together when factors measure almost the same thing (e.g. inhabitants and establishments).

blockers.noData: Load datasets first: the optimisation compares the columns of the table.
blockers.noEntities: Select at least one place (at least four for meaningful results).

result.title: Result: {name}
result.stale: This result is outdated (settings or table changed). Recalculate to update it.
result.unitNote: Scale: the mean of the formula equals the mean of “{factor}”. Scaled values are therefore “per equivalent” of that quantity.
result.cvExplain: Cross-validated means: every place is scaled with a formula that never saw it. This number is more honest than the fitted one; a large gap between the two shows overfitting. CV = standard deviation / mean of the scaled values (smaller = more comparable).
result.selectionInfo: {tried} combinations of {candidates} candidates tried ({method}). Best cross-validated error for 1, 2, 3 … factors:
result.selectionRule: The smallest combination whose error is at most 5 % above the best one is chosen.
result.accountsLegend: Per account: CV unscaled → CV fitted / CV cross-validated, cross-validated improvement.

warn.fewEntities: Only {count} places: every figure is uncertain. Load more columns before applying the formula.
warn.overfitRisk: Overfitting risk: {risk}. The formula may only fit these places.
warn.selectionOptimism: The factors were chosen among {tried} combinations on the same few places, so the cross-validated error is likely too optimistic.
warn.cvWorseThanUnscaled: Cross-validated, the formula is worse than not scaling at all.
warn.nonPositiveScale: For {count} place(ies) the formula is not positive: they cannot be scaled.
warn.negativeCoefficient: The formula contains negative weights (least-squares method). “Non-negative” is easier to interpret.
warn.collinearFactors: Skipped because they follow exactly from other factors: {factors}.
warn.tooManyFactors: {factors} factors for only {places} places: without automatic selection overfitting is certain.
warn.notConverged: The calculation did not fully converge; the result is approximate.

account.tooFewEntities: Account {name}: fewer than two places with a value.
account.mixedSign: Account {name}: mixed positive and negative values, cannot be scaled.
account.mostlyZero: Account {name}: zero for more than half of the places.
account.noVariation: Account {name}: identical for all places, nothing to compare.

entity.noAccountData: {name}: left out, no value in the chosen accounts.

failure.tooFewEntities: At least two places with data are needed: a single column has nothing to be compared with.
failure.noUsableAccounts: None of the accounts ({codes}) can be scaled: not found, or too little data, mixed signs or constant values.
failure.noUsableFactors: No scaling factor has usable data for the selected places.
failure.singular: No formula can be determined with the chosen factors.
failure.noEffect: None of the factors receives a positive weight.

compare.title: Scenarios compared
compare.hint: The smaller the cross-validated CV, the more comparable the places are after scaling.
compare.footnote: CV with formula: cross-validated (fitted in brackets). Scenarios with different accounts or places are only partly comparable.

sim.title: Simulations
sim.intro: Keep calculating with the selected formula without refitting anything.

whatIf.intro: Enter factor values of a municipality that does not (yet) exist and see which amounts the formula expects.
whatIf.notPositive: For these values the formula is not positive: no prediction possible.
whatIf.footnote: Range = expected amount ± typical deviation of an unseen place (the account’s cross-validated CV). The dot marks the actual amount of the reference place.

expected.intro: Who spends unusually much or little for their size? The expected amount comes from a formula that did not know the place.
expected.footnote: Deviation = actual / expected − 1. Rank 1 = furthest above expectation. A deviation is not a verdict: it may also reflect missing factors or different tasks.

sensitivity.intro: What happens to the expectation and to a place’s rank if a factor were 10 % or 25 % smaller or larger?
sensitivity.legend: Per cell: change of the factor, change of the expected amount, rank before → after.
sensitivity.unavailable: There are no values for this selection.

restOfCanton.title: Calculated figures: "Other municipalities"
restOfCanton.text: Nobody publishes figures for the remaining municipalities of a canton (under 5,000 inhabitants). They were calculated here: the figures of all municipalities of the canton minus the individual municipalities with 5,000 or more inhabitants. This is an approximation.
restOfCanton.limits: Payments between municipalities (accounts 361–363 and 461–463) and accounts that cannot be subtracted cleanly are missing. Totals and profit/loss are therefore only partly comparable with other columns. There is no breakdown by area of responsibility.

wizard.intro: Four steps: choose places, choose years, decide how to convert the amounts, then see the result as charts or a table.

places.title: Which places do you want to compare?
places.help: Search for municipalities, cantons, the federal government or a social insurance and add them. The order here is the order in the charts and the table.

years.title: Which years?
years.help: One year shows the places side by side. Several years also show how the numbers developed. The conversion uses each year’s own statistics.
years.customCombination: The link has its own mix of places and years. As soon as you pick a year here, it applies to all places.

scaling.title: How should the amounts be converted?
scaling.help: Big places have big amounts. Dividing by the number of inhabitants or another statistic makes places of different size comparable. Below you see what each column is divided by.

preview.title: How the amounts are converted
preview.introStat: Each column is divided by “{name}” ({unit}) of its place and year:
preview.introFormula: Each column is divided by the result of the formula “{formula}” for its place and year:
preview.otherYears: A small year means the statistic does not exist for that year; the nearest year is used.
preview.missingNote: Where the statistic is missing, the column stays in francs and is left out of the charts.

charts.empty: Nothing to show for this choice.
charts.lineKeyboardHint: Use the arrow keys to go from year to year.
charts.skippedUnscaled: No statistic for the conversion, so not in the charts: {names}. In the table these columns are in francs.

trend.title: Development: {measure}
trend.subtitle: {from} to {to}, {unit}
trend.capped: The chart shows the first {count} of {total} places; the table has all of them.

result.title: Result: surplus or deficit
result.note: Revenue minus expenses. Blue means more came in than went out, red less.

revenueStructure.title: Where does the money come from?
revenueStructure.note: Taxes are income, wealth and profit taxes. Transfers are contributions from the federal government, the canton or other municipalities. Fees pay for things like waste or water.

expenseStructure.title: What is the money spent on?
expenseStructure.note: Transfers are contributions to others, for example to schools, hospitals, social assistance or fiscal equalisation. Goods and services is everything that is bought in.

charts.netDebtNote: Net debt = liabilities minus financial assets. A negative value means the financial assets exceed the debt (net assets).
